GPSR Compressed Sensing Algorithm

Source: R/pp_decode.R
pp_gpsr.Rd

Solves the \(\ell_1\)-regularized least squares problem for scoring candidate samples when COMP produces too many candidates.

Usage

pp_gpsr(
  A,
  y,
  tau = NULL,
  max_iter = 500L,
  tol = 1e-05,
  continuation_steps = 5L,
  first_tau_factor = 0.8
)

Arguments

A

Numeric design matrix with dimensions \(J \times N\). In the decoding pipeline it is typically the submatrix of positive pools by candidate individuals, but any numeric matrix is allowed.

y

Numeric vector of length \(J\) containing the observed response associated with A. In the decoding pipeline this is usually a vector of normalized pool intensities or binary positive-pool indicators.

tau

Numeric non-negative regularization scalar or NULL. When NULL (default), \(\tau\) is computed from the data as $$\tau = 0.005 \cdot \max|\mathbf{A}^T \mathbf{y}|$$ using the package's default GPSR scaling. Supply a positive numeric value to override the data-adaptive default. Larger values promote sparser solutions.

max_iter

Integer scalar giving the maximum number of projected-gradient iterations. The default is 500L.

tol

Numeric scalar giving the convergence tolerance for the relative change in objective value. The default is 1e-5. Convergence is declared when \(|F(\mathbf{z}_{\text{new}}) - F(\mathbf{z})| / \max(1, |F(\mathbf{z})|) < \texttt{tol}\).

continuation_steps

Integer scalar giving the number of warm-start continuation steps before the main loop. The default is 5L.

first_tau_factor

Numeric scalar giving the scale factor that determines the starting regularization in the continuation schedule. The default is 0.8. It sets the continuation starting value through \(\tau_{\text{start}} = \texttt{first\_tau\_factor} \cdot \max|\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{y}|\).

Value

A list with components:

x

Numeric vector; the estimated sparse solution

iterations

Integer; number of iterations performed

converged

Logical; TRUE if converged before max_iter

Details

GPSR (Gradient Projection for Sparse Reconstruction) solves the convex optimization problem $$ \min_{\mathbf{x} \geq 0} \frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}\|_2^2 + \tau\|\mathbf{x}\|_1. $$ The \(\ell_1\) penalty promotes sparse solutions while the non-negativity constraint keeps the candidate scores interpretable as non-negative weights.

Algorithm

The implementation follows a GPSR-BB style projected-gradient scheme with a short continuation warm start. Let \(F_\tau(\mathbf{z}) = \frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{A}\mathbf{z} - \mathbf{y}\|_2^2 + \tau \mathbf{1}^T\mathbf{z}\) with gradient \(\nabla F_\tau(\mathbf{z}) = \mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}\mathbf{z} - \mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{y} + \tau\mathbf{1}\). Before the main loop, the algorithm applies continuation_steps projected-gradient updates at geometrically decreasing regularization values from $$ \tau_{\text{start}} = \texttt{first\_tau\_factor} \cdot \max|\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{y}| $$ down to the target \(\tau\). The main loop then alternates gradient evaluation, projection onto the non-negative orthant, backtracking line search, and a Barzilai-Borwein step-size update. Convergence is declared when $$ \frac{|F_\tau(\mathbf{z}_{k+1}) - F_\tau(\mathbf{z}_k)|}{ \max(1, |F_\tau(\mathbf{z}_k)|) } < \texttt{tol}. $$

Role in Decoding

When COMP produces more candidates than \(k_{\max}\), GPSR assigns continuous scores to those candidates. Larger scores indicate stronger support for inclusion in a sparse positive set, but the scores themselves are not final binary calls.

References

Figueiredo, M. A. T., Nowak, R. D., & Wright, S. J. (2007). Gradient Projection for Sparse Reconstruction. IEEE Journal of Selected Topics in Signal Processing, 1(4), 586-597.

Kim, H. Y., Hudgens, M. G., Dreyfuss, J. M., Westreich, D. J., & Pilcher, C. D. (2007). Comparison of group testing algorithms for case identification in the presence of test error. Biometrics, 63(4), 1152-1163.

See also

pp_comp, pp_decode, pp_matrix

Other decoding: decoding_algorithms, pp_comp(), pp_decode(), pp_validate()

Examples

# Simple example
A <- matrix(c(1, 1, 0,
              0, 1, 1,
              1, 0, 1), nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE)
A
#>      [,1] [,2] [,3]
#> [1,]    1    1    0
#> [2,]    0    1    1
#> [3,]    1    0    1
y <- c(1, 0.8, 0.5)
y
#> [1] 1.0 0.8 0.5

result <- pp_gpsr(A, y)          # tau computed from data
result
#> $x
#> [1] 0.3481352 0.6382880 0.1723102
#> 
#> $iterations
#> [1] 9
#> 
#> $converged
#> [1] TRUE
#> 
result$x
#> [1] 0.3481352 0.6382880 0.1723102
result$converged
#> [1] TRUE

# Typical use: score candidates from COMP
M <- pp_matrix(q = 8, d = 3, nl = 6, N = 384)
M
#> 48 x 384 sparse Matrix of class "dgCMatrix"
